routines.name: _id_list
routines.docstring:
Read an optional array-of-change-id field, defaulting to empty.

SPEC: depends_on/applied must be arrays of nonempty strings. Shape errors are
rejected here so graph code can trust the values it receives.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate change records and collapse identical duplicates.

Returns dicts {"id","component","units","depends_on"} in first-appearance
order. SPEC: duplicates are identical only when id, component, units and the
*set* of dependencies match, hence frozenset(deps) in the dedup key; any other
repeat of an id is conflicting-change. Deduplication runs before accounting
and graph construction so repeated records are never counted twice.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Validate the persisted release journal against the known change set.

`applied` defaults to empty. Unknown ids mean the caller's journal does not
describe this release set, so replay and ordering would be unsound; SPEC maps
that to unknown-dependency (not invalid-change). Malformed shape stays
invalid-change via _id_list.

comments: # Same id but different identity: the caller's intent is ambiguous, so
# neither record may be chosen silently on its behalf.
# Sorted unique: replay is a set of states, and a repeated id must not make
# rollback emit the same action twice or plan count it twice.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

Import direction: journal.py is a leaf module (imports nothing local). It owns
record validation, identity/replay semantics and existence checks; it never
orders changes. planner.py calls it and then ranks the graph.

Every rejection raises JournalError carrying the SPEC error code as its message,
so planner converts it into the failure object without inspecting types.

routines.name: failure
routines.docstring: The single failure shape from SPEC: no partial actions, units always 0.

routines.name: _topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return every change id in deterministic topological order.

Raises unknown-dependency for dependency targets that are not change ids and
dependency-cycle when any part of the graph is cyclic (including components
with cycles unreachable from an acyclic prefix).

Tie-breaking: among changes whose dependencies are all already emitted, the
lexicographically smallest id goes next. heapq gives that deterministically,
so the same request always yields the same order regardless of input order.
The full order is computed even for `plan` because rollback reverses it and
plan must still reject cycles it would otherwise only reach via unapplied
records.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring:
Validate the request and build the ordered action list.

Order matters: request shape, then policy (environment/action/budget), then
journal identity/applied, then graph. Every check raises before any action is
assembled, so a rejected request can never emit partial actions.

comments: # A missing target means the caller's graph references a change this
# request cannot describe, so no safe order exists.
# A self-dependency can never be satisfied; treat as a cycle
# instead of silently ignoring the record.
# Fewer emitted ids than changes means the leftover set holds or feeds a
# cycle; SPEC requires a cycle anywhere to fail, applied or not.
# Rollback walks the full deterministic order backwards and emits only
# what the journal says is live. SPEC: budget is validated but never caps
# a rollback, since undoing work is the recovery path.
# plan: applied entries already satisfy their dependencies and cost nothing, so
# they are skipped both as output and in the budget sum decided below.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Import direction: planner.py is the top of the local stack (journal.py and
policy.py import nothing local). It owns graph validation, ordering and the
result assembly, and is the only module that builds success/failure objects.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the validated budget for an already-confirmed object request.

Checks run in a fixed order (environment, action, budget) so a request with
several defects always reports the same first code. Raises PolicyError whose
message is the SPEC error code; planner turns it into the failure object.

comments: # G1 grants both environments plan and rollback; the table stays explicit because
# a later goal (CHANGE-G2.md) may narrow one environment without touching the rest.
# isinstance(str) is checked first: dict/list values from JSON are unhashable
# and would raise TypeError inside the membership test, turning a domain error
# into a crashed process (SPEC: every request exits normally with JSON).
# A known environment with an action this goal does not implement is rejected
# here, before journal/planner work, so no partial actions are ever emitted.
# Same unhashable guard as above for non-string actions.
# type(...) is int (not isinstance) so booleans are not accepted as integers.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Import direction: policy.py is a leaf module (imports nothing local). It owns the
environment/action/budget gate only; record identity, graph and ordering stay in
journal and planner, so a policy rejection happens before any journal or graph
work and cannot leave partial actions behind.

routines.name: _retained
routines.docstring:
Return the staging rollback retention closure (G2).

`retain` lists applied ids that must stay. Its transitive dependencies are kept
only when they are themselves applied: an unapplied dependency is not part of
the live release, so keeping it would make the emitted rollback describe state
that was never there. Retained ids (and their closure) are therefore left out
of the reverse order emitted by the caller.

Malformed shape (non-array, non-string or empty ids) and ids that are not in
the applied journal are both invalid-retain: the caller asked to preserve
something this request cannot preserve. This replaces the generic
invalid-change that _id_list would raise, because CHANGE-G2 names the code.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring:
Validate the request and build the ordered action list.

Order matters: request shape, then policy (environment/action/budget + the G2
production freeze), then journal identity/applied, then graph, then rollback
retention. Every check raises before any action is assembled, so a rejected
request can never emit partial actions. budget is already the effective one, so
the staging plan cap from G2 lives entirely in policy.py.

comments: # A missing target means the caller's graph references a change this
# request cannot describe, so no safe order exists.
# A self-dependency can never be satisfied; treat as a cycle
# instead of silently ignoring the record.
# Fewer emitted ids than changes means the leftover set holds or feeds a
# cycle; SPEC requires a cycle anywhere to fail, applied or not.
# Iterative walk with an explicit stack: a deep chain must not hit the recursion
# limit and crash the transport (SPEC: every request exits with JSON).
# Rollback walks the full deterministic order backwards and emits only
# what the journal says is live. SPEC: budget is validated but never caps
# a rollback, since undoing work is the recovery path. G2 retention is
# computed here, after the graph is known valid, because the closure needs
# the dependencies of already-checked changes.
# plan: applied entries already satisfy their dependencies and cost nothing, so
# they are skipped both as output and in the budget sum decided below. `retain`
# is a rollback-only field (CHANGE-G2), so a malformed retain is ignored here.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Import direction: planner.py is the top of the local stack (journal.py and
policy.py import nothing local). It owns graph validation, ordering and the
result assembly, and is the only module that builds success/failure objects.

routines.name: check_environment
routines.docstring:
Validate `environment` and enforce the G2 production freeze.

This gate runs before action/budget/journal/graph checks on purpose: a frozen
environment must answer production-frozen even when changes or applied are
malformed, and it must never emit partial actions. Raises PolicyError whose
message is the SPEC/CHANGE-G2 error code.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the validated budget for an already-confirmed object request.

Checks run in a fixed order (environment + freeze, action, budget) so a request
with several defects always reports the same first code. Raises PolicyError
whose message is the SPEC/CHANGE-G2 error code; planner turns it into the
failure object. The returned budget is the effective one: for a staging plan it
is already capped at STAGING_PLAN_CAP.

comments: # G2 is staging-only: production is frozen for every action, so it intentionally
# has no allowed actions here. The table stays explicit per environment so a later
# goal can re-open one environment without touching the other.
# G2 refuses production before any graph/change validation, so the planner can
# still return production-frozen for a malformed request instead of the deeper
# graph error. Both plan and rollback are frozen.
# G2 caps a staging plan at 3 units regardless of the requested budget; the
# request itself is still validated as a nonnegative integer first.
# isinstance(str) is checked first: dict/list values from JSON are unhashable
# and would raise TypeError inside the membership test, turning a domain error
# into a crashed process (SPEC: every request exits normally with JSON).
# A known environment with an action this goal does not implement is rejected
# here, before journal/planner work, so no partial actions are ever emitted.
# Same unhashable guard as above for non-string actions.
# type(...) is int (not isinstance) so booleans are not accepted as integers.
# G2: a staging plan may emit at most min(request budget, 3) units; the request
# value alone never raises the cap. Rollback keeps the raw budget (validated,
# never capping), so the cap is applied to plan only.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

journal and planner, so a policy rejection happens before any journal or graph
